Theme

Nature & food

sky noun

also skies

classical

Cic. Tusc. 1.43: caelum hoc, in quō nūbēs, imbrēs, ventīque cōguntur
Cic. ND 2.4: cum caelum suspeximus
Traupman 136

caelum, caelī n.

noun, second declension

sky, heaven

The sky, and the weather in it (serēnum caelum, a clear sky; see clear sky); caelum suspicere, to look up at the sky. The plural caelī, the heavens, is poetic and Church Latin (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Quid sī nunc caelum ruat?

    What if the sky fell in right now? (said of a needless fear)Ter. Heaut. 719

  • prōnaque cum spectent animālia cētera terram, ōs hominī sublīme dedit, caelumque vidēre jussit et ērēctōs ad sīdera tollere vultūs

    while the other animals look down at the ground, he gave man an upturned face, and bade him look at the sky and lift his eyes to the starsOv. Met. 1.84–86

  • Crepusculō caelum prīmum rubēbat, tum violāceum fīēbat, postrēmō nigrum

    At dusk the sky was red at first, then turned violet, and at last blackLibellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum

See also cloud, clear sky, sun, moon, star.

SourcesLewis & Short: caelum

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 136.

Terence and Cicero checked against the Latin Library text (CLTK mirror); Ovid from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-ovidius).

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 9 November 2026. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word.
